full_title: ATTY. RIZA S. FERNANDEZ, PETITIONER, VS. WILLIE FERNANDO MAALIW, RESPONDENT.

doctrine:
**A decision of the Civil Service Commission dismissing an administrative complaint for lack of a prima facie case is appealable to the Court of Appeals by petition for review under Rule 43**, consistent with Section 9(3) of BP 129 and Section 73, Rule 13 of the RRACCS. The non-appealability rules invoked do not apply: Section 47, Book V, Title I of the Administrative Code of 1987 covers decisions of department secretaries or agency heads imposing suspension of not more than 30 days or a fine not exceeding 30 days' salary, and Section 72 of the RRACCS covers decisions of agencies that would otherwise be appealable to the CSC.

**The private complainant may appeal the CSC decision in appropriate cases.** The RRACCS provisions on elevating decisions of the CSC and its Regional Offices use the generic term "party" (or "either by the complainant or the respondent"), not "party adversely affected," which the RRACCS uses only for motions for reconsideration in disciplinary cases and appeals in non-disciplinary cases. The *Mendez v. CSC* line limiting appeals to the party adversely affected was overruled in *CSC v. Dacoycoy*, and *PNB v. Garcia* and *Constantino-David v. Pangandaman-Gania* recognized the private complainant's standing.

**A court violates administrative due process when it finds a civil servant administratively liable although no Formal Charge was issued and she was never allowed to answer and be investigated under the RRACCS** (*Ang Tibay*; *Salva v. Valle*). At most, the court may find a prima facie case and let the disciplining authority proceed. Finally, **a violation of a complainant's right to speedy disposition of cases does not ipso facto make the personnel in charge liable**, especially those whose employment began long after the case was filed or submitted for resolution; responsibility lies with the agency as an institution, where it sufficiently explains that the delay was not attributable to the individual (applying *Navarro v. COA*).
facts:
On September 28, 1999, respondent Willie Fernando Maaliw filed an administrative complaint for grave misconduct, oppression, dishonesty, negligence, and violation of RA 6713 and the Civil Service Law against his co-employee Danilo Longasa, a Special Investigator at the Land Bank of the Philippines. The complaint was submitted for decision on January 21, 2000. On June 16, 2014, more than 14 years later, the CSC-National Capital Region (CSC-NCR) dismissed it for being insufficient in form. The decision was signed by Director Lydia Castillo and prepared by petitioner Atty. Riza S. Fernandez.

Because of the delay, Maaliw filed a Complaint-Affidavit dated November 9, 2015 against Fernandez and Dir. Castillo for neglect of duty and violation of RA 6713 before the Office of the Ombudsman, which referred it to the CSC. In their Joint Comment, they said the complaint had been pending long before they took their posts: Dir. Castillo was reassigned to the Legal Services Division (LSD) of the CSC-NCR only on December 6, 2012 precisely to reduce aged cases, and Fernandez was employed only on February 11, 2013. They cited the volume of cases and the LSD's limited personnel, and noted that Maaliw never sought reconsideration of or appealed the 2014 dismissal.

On August 31, 2016, the CSC dismissed Maaliw's complaint. It recognized that the 14-year delay violated Maaliw's right to a speedy disposition of his case, but held that the delay could not be attributed to Fernandez and Dir. Castillo and was justified by the caseload of the LSD's eight personnel. Reconsideration was denied on December 16, 2016.

On Maaliw's Rule 43 petition, the CA (Decision of January 14, 2019) reversed the CSC and found Fernandez and Dir. Castillo guilty of simple neglect of duty, fining each an amount equal to three months' salary in lieu of suspension since both had left the CSC-NCR. It faulted Fernandez for her inaction during the one year and six months after she assumed her post and rejected lack of manpower as an excuse. Dir. Castillo did not timely move for reconsideration. Fernandez's motion was denied on July 26, 2019, and she filed a Rule 45 petition, arguing that the CSC decision was not appealable, that Maaliw had no personality to appeal, that she was found guilty without a Formal Charge, and that she acted on the complaint within days.
issues: Whether a CSC decision dismissing an administrative complaint for lack of a prima facie case may be appealed to the CA by petition for review under Rule 43.
Whether Maaliw, as the private complainant, had personality to appeal the CSC decision.
Whether the CA violated Fernandez's right to due process by finding her guilty of simple neglect of duty without a Formal Charge.
Whether Fernandez is liable for the 14-year delay in resolving Maaliw's complaint against Longasa.
ruling:
At the outset, the petition raised questions of law (the proper remedy, due process, and liability on the facts already presented), and in any case fell within the exceptions allowing factual review, since it alleged a denial of due process and the CSC and CA findings conflicted.

**1. Yes.** The complaint against Fernandez was instituted directly with the CSC, so Section 72, Rule 13 of the RRACCS, which refers to non-appealable decisions of agencies that would ordinarily be appealable to the CSC, does not apply. Section 47, Book V, Title I of the Administrative Code makes non-appealable only decisions of department secretaries or agency heads imposing suspension of not more than 30 days or a fine of not more than 30 days' salary; a CSC dismissal for lack of a prima facie case is not covered. Section 48(2) is silent on whether such a dismissal is appealable. **The CSC decision is appealable to the CA under Rule 43**, consistent with Section 9(3) of BP 129, Section 1 of Rule 43 (which names the CSC), and Section 73, Rule 13 of the RRACCS.

**2. Yes.** Fernandez relied on portions of *Light Rail Transit Authority v. Salvaña* repeating *Mendez v. CSC*, which limited appeals to the "party adversely affected," but those pronouncements were expressly overruled in *CSC v. Dacoycoy*. In *PNB v. Garcia*, the Court held that "the campaign against corruption, malfeasance and misfeasance in government will be undermined if the government or the private offended party is prevented from appealing erroneous administrative decisions"; in *Constantino-David*, that the CSC's right to appeal "does not preclude the private complainant in appropriate cases from similarly elevating the decision for review." The RRACCS uses "party adversely affected" only in Sections 56 and 111; Section 73 provides that "[a] party may elevate" a CSC decision to the CA, and Section 71 allows CSC Regional Office decisions to be elevated "either by the complainant or the respondent." **This was an "appropriate case" for the private complainant to appeal.**

**3. Yes, Fernandez was denied due process.** Under *Ang Tibay*, the first right in administrative proceedings is the right to a hearing. Before being held liable, Fernandez should have been issued a Formal Charge (Rule 5, RRACCS), allowed to file an Answer (Rule 6), and possibly given a formal investigation (Rule 8). The CSC's order to comment was not a Formal Charge. As in *Salva v. Valle*, without a formal charge and proper investigation, the respondent could not defend herself and the truth could not be reasonably ascertained. **"At most, what the CA could have ruled is that there is a prima facie case against Fernandez, thereby allowing the CSC to conduct further proceedings in relation to Maaliw's complaint."**

**4. No.** Nonetheless, given the undisputed facts, the Court agreed with the CSC that there was no prima facie case. **Liability for delay "does not ipso facto attach" to LSD members in charge of the complaint, "more so to members whose employment commenced much later" than its filing or submission for resolution; responsibility for the violation of the right to speedy disposition lies on the CSC as an institution.** Applying *Navarro v. COA* (factors: length of delay, reasons, assertion of the right, and prejudice), the CSC sufficiently explained that the delay was not attributable to Fernandez: it admitted the violation as an institution and supported the heavy caseload with data on carry-over, ripe and pending cases from 2012 to 2014. The Court also denied Maaliw's request to investigate Fernandez for violating Canons 1 and 12 of the Code of Professional Responsibility, reminding him that allegations against members of the bar must have clear factual and legal basis.
disposition: Petition GRANTED. The CA Decision of January 14, 2019 and Resolution of July 26, 2019 in CA-G.R. SP No. 149279 were REVERSED and SET ASIDE. The CSC Decision of August 31, 2016 and Resolution of December 16, 2016 in CC-D-2015-021, dismissing Maaliw's complaint, were REINSTATED.

bar_questions.q: Carlo filed an administrative complaint for grave misconduct directly with the Civil Service Commission against Dina, an employee of a CSC regional office. The CSC dismissed the complaint for lack of a prima facie case. Carlo filed a petition for review under Rule 43 with the Court of Appeals. Dina moved to dismiss, arguing that (1) a CSC decision dismissing a complaint for lack of a prima facie case is not appealable, and (2) only the "party adversely affected," meaning a respondent found guilty, may appeal, so Carlo, as complainant, has no personality to appeal. Rule on Dina's motion.

alac.answer: The motion should be denied. The CSC decision is appealable to the CA under Rule 43, and Carlo, as private complainant, has personality to appeal.
alac.legal_basis: Under Section 9(3) of BP 129, Section 1 of Rule 43 of the Rules of Court, and Section 73, Rule 13 of the RRACCS, decisions of the CSC are appealable to the CA by petition for review. Section 47, Book V, Title I of the Administrative Code makes non-appealable only decisions of department secretaries or agency heads imposing suspension of not more than 30 days or a fine not exceeding 30 days' salary; a dismissal for lack of a prima facie case is not covered. The RRACCS allows "a party" to elevate CSC decisions; the Mendez line limiting appeals to the "party adversely affected" was overruled in CSC v. Dacoycoy, and the private complainant may appeal in appropriate cases (PNB v. Garcia; Constantino-David v. Pangandaman-Gania). (Fernandez v. Maaliw, G.R. No. 248852, March 9, 2022)
alac.application: Carlo's complaint was filed directly with the CSC, and the CSC's dismissal does not fall under the non-appealability rule for minor penalties imposed by department or agency heads. Rule 43 expressly names the CSC among the agencies whose decisions go to the CA. As complainant, Carlo is a "party" under the RRACCS, and barring him from appealing would undermine the campaign against misconduct in government.
alac.conclusion: Carlo correctly appealed to the CA under Rule 43 and has personality to do so, so Dina's motion should be denied.

bar_questions.q: In the same case, the Court of Appeals found that Carlo's evidence against Dina was strong. Instead of remanding the case, it reversed the CSC and directly found Dina guilty of simple neglect of duty, fining her three months' salary. The CSC had only required Dina to comment on the complaint; it never issued a Formal Charge or conducted an investigation. Is the CA's ruling valid?

alac.answer: No. The CA violated Dina's right to administrative due process.
alac.legal_basis: Under Ang Tibay v. Court of Industrial Relations, the first of the primary rights in administrative proceedings is the right to a hearing, which includes the right to present one's case and submit evidence. Under the RRACCS, a respondent must first be issued a Formal Charge, allowed to file an Answer, and, where warranted, given a formal investigation before being held liable. An order to comment is not a Formal Charge. Where the disciplining authority dismissed the complaint for lack of a prima facie case, the most the appellate court may do is find a prima facie case and allow the CSC to conduct further proceedings. (Fernandez v. Maaliw, G.R. No. 248852, March 9, 2022, citing Salva v. Valle)
alac.application: Dina was never formally charged, never filed an Answer to a Formal Charge, and was never investigated. A comment on the complaint does not give her the full opportunity to defend herself that the RRACCS requires. However strong the evidence appeared, the CA could at most rule that a prima facie case exists and let the CSC proceed with the Formal Charge and investigation.
alac.conclusion: The CA's finding of guilt is void for violating due process; it could only have found a prima facie case and allowed the CSC to proceed.

bar_questions.q: A complaint filed in 2008 sat unresolved in a CSC regional office until 2024, when it was dismissed. Atty. Ella, a hearing officer, joined that office only in 2023 and prepared the 2024 resolution. The CSC admitted that the 16-year delay violated the complainant's right to a speedy disposition of his case, but showed, with data on carry-over and pending cases, that the delay was caused by the office's huge backlog and few lawyers. The complainant charges Atty. Ella with neglect of duty because of the delay. Is Atty. Ella administratively liable?

alac.answer: No. Atty. Ella is not liable; responsibility for the delay lies with the CSC as an institution.
alac.legal_basis: Article III, Section 16 of the Constitution guarantees a speedy disposition of cases before administrative bodies. But a violation of this right does not ipso facto make the members of the office in charge of the case liable, more so those whose employment began long after the case was filed or submitted for resolution. Responsibility lies on the agency as an institution where it sufficiently explains that the delay was not attributable to the individual, considering the length of the delay, the reasons for it, the assertion of the right, and the prejudice caused (Navarro v. COA). (Fernandez v. Maaliw, G.R. No. 248852, March 9, 2022)
alac.application: Almost all of the 16-year delay happened before Atty. Ella joined the office in 2023. The CSC admitted its institutional responsibility and explained, with data, that the delay came from its backlog and lack of personnel, not from Atty. Ella's neglect. As in Fernandez, where the lawyer who joined only in 2013 and prepared the 2014 decision was absolved of a 14-year delay, the facts show no prima facie case of neglect against Atty. Ella.
alac.conclusion: Atty. Ella cannot be held liable for neglect of duty for a delay that is attributable to the CSC as an institution.

notes: Section numbers of the RRACCS are as cited in the Decision, which refers to both the 2011 RRACCS and the 2017 RACCS (e.g., Section 71, formerly Section 67). Dir. Castillo did not timely move for reconsideration of the CA Decision and was not a party to the petition; the fallo reinstates the CSC Decision without separately addressing her. The Decision's footnotes on the cases cited for the "party adversely affected" discussion contain cross-reference numbering that does not match the notes they point to; the case names in the text were relied on.
